column2: The organization's cybersecurity risk management strategy, expectations, and policy are established, communicated, and monitored

The circumstances - mission, stakeholder expectations, dependencies, and legal, regulatory, and contractual requirements - surrounding the organization's cybersecurity risk management decisions are understood
The organizational mission is understood and informs cybersecurity risk management
Internal and external stakeholders are understood, and their needs and expectations regarding cybersecurity risk management are understood and considered
Legal, regulatory, and contractual requirements regarding cybersecurity - including privacy and civil liberties obligations - are understood and managed
Critical objectives, capabilities, and services that external stakeholders depend on or expect from the organization are understood and communicated
Outcomes, capabilities, and services that the organization depends on are understood and communicated
The organization's priorities, constraints, risk tolerance and appetite statements, and assumptions are established, communicated, and used to support operational risk decisions
Risk management objectives are established and agreed to by organizational stakeholders
Risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated, and maintained
Cybersecurity risk management activities and outcomes are included in enterprise risk management processes
Strategic direction that describes appropriate risk response options is established and communicated
Lines of communication across the organization are established for cybersecurity risks, including risks from suppliers and other third parties
A standardized method for calculating, documenting, categorizing, and prioritizing cybersecurity risks is established and communicated
Strategic opportunities (i.e., positive risks) are characterized and are included in organizational cybersecurity risk discussions
Cybersecurity roles, responsibilities, and authorities to foster accountability, performance assessment, and continuous improvement are established and communicated
Organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical, and continually improving
Roles, responsibilities, and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood, and enforced
Adequate resources are allocated commensurate with the cybersecurity risk strategy, roles, responsibilities, and policies
Cybersecurity is included in human resources practices
Organizational cybersecurity policy is established, communicated, and enforced
Policy for managing cybersecurity risks is established based on organizational context, cybersecurity strategy, and priorities and is communicated and enforced
Policy for managing cybersecurity risks is reviewed, updated, communicated, and enforced to reflect changes in requirements, threats, technology, and organizational mission
Results of organization-wide cybersecurity risk management activities and performance are used to inform, improve, and adjust the risk management strategy
Cybersecurity risk management strategy outcomes are reviewed to inform and adjust strategy and direction
The cybersecurity risk management strategy is reviewed and adjusted to ensure coverage of organizational requirements and risks
Organizational cybersecurity risk management performance is evaluated and reviewed for adjustments needed
Cyber supply chain risk management processes are identified, established, managed, monitored, and improved by organizational stakeholders
A cybersecurity supply chain risk management program, strategy, objectives, policies, and processes are established and agreed to by organizational stakeholders
Cybersecurity roles and responsibilities for suppliers, customers, and partners are established, communicated, and coordinated internally and externally
Cybersecurity supply chain risk management is integrated into cybersecurity and enterprise risk management, risk assessment, and improvement processes
Suppliers are known and prioritized by criticality
Requirements to address cybersecurity risks in supply chains are established, prioritized, and integrated into contracts and other types of agreements with suppliers and other relevant third parties
Planning and due diligence are performed to reduce risks before entering into formal supplier or other third-party relationships
The risks posed by a supplier, their products and services, and other third parties are understood, recorded, prioritized, assessed, responded to, and monitored over the course of the relationship
column6: Verify that provider model, version, or routing changes trigger security re-evaluation before continued use.
column7: Triggering security re-evaluation when a provider changes the model, version or routing is the AI-specific part of monitoring supplier products for risk-profile changes; without it GV.SC-07 is not met for provider-hosted models.
column8: The change originates at the supplier (GV.SC-07 Ex4). Precedent: SA-9, SR-6 -> GV.SC-07.

column2: Relevant suppliers and other third parties are included in incident planning, response, and recovery activities
Supply chain security practices are integrated into cybersecurity and enterprise risk management programs, and their performance is monitored throughout the technology product and service life cycle
Cybersecurity supply chain risk management plans include provisions for activities that occur after the conclusion of a partnership or service agreement
The organization's current cybersecurity risks are understood

Assets (e.g., data, hardware, software, systems, facilities, services, people) that enable the organization to achieve business purposes are identified and managed consistent with their relative importance to organizational objectives and the organization's risk strategy
Inventories of hardware managed by the organization are maintained
Inventories of software, services, and systems managed by the organization are maintained
column6: Verify that a model registry maintains an inventory of all deployed model artifacts and their origin.
column7: Maintaining a model registry of all deployed model artifacts and their origin is the AI-specific part of maintaining software inventories; without it ID.AM-02 is not met for deployed models.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 CM-8 and PM-5 to ID.AM-02.

column2: Inventories of software, services, and systems managed by the organization are maintained
column6: Verify that fine-tuning checkpoints are registered as distinct artifacts.
column7: Registering fine-tuning checkpoints as distinct artifacts is one way to extend the inventory of software managed by the organization to intermediate model artifacts produced during fine-tuning.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 CM-8 to ID.AM-02. 'example of': ID.AM-02 can be met for deployed models without registering every intermediate checkpoint.

column2: Inventories of software, services, and systems managed by the organization are maintained
column6: Verify that every model artifact publishes a version-controlled, machine-readable AI BOM listing datasets, weights, licenses, and data-origin statements.
column7: Publishing a version-controlled, machine-readable AI BOM for every model artifact is one way to maintain an inventory of AI software and its components.
column8: The AI BOM inventories model artifacts and components first; dataset provenance is a part of it. Precedent: CM-8 -> ID.AM-02.

column2: Inventories of software, services, and systems managed by the organization are maintained
column6: Verify that AI BOM completeness checks fail the build if any component metadata is missing.
column7: Automated AI BOM completeness checks are one way to keep the inventory of AI software components complete and accurate.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 CM-8 to ID.AM-02.

column2: Representations of the organization's authorized network communication and internal and external network data flows are maintained
Inventories of services provided by suppliers are maintained
Assets are prioritized based on classification, criticality, resources, and impact on the mission
Inventories of data and corresponding metadata for designated data types are maintained
column6: Verify that an up-to-date inventory is kept of every training-data source, including its origin, responsible party, license, collection method, intended use constraints, and processing history.
column7: Keeping an up-to-date inventory of every training-data source with origin, responsible party and processing history is the AI-specific part of maintaining data inventories with provenance and owner metadata; without it ID.AM-07 is not met for training data.
column8: Matches ID.AM-07 Ex4 (track provenance and data owner). Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 CM-12 and CM-13 to ID.AM-07.

column2: Inventories of data and corresponding metadata for designated data types are maintained
column6: Verify that data classification labels propagate to downstream resources (embeddings, prompt caches, model outputs).
column7: Propagating data classification labels to embeddings, prompt caches and model outputs is one way to keep classification metadata attached to AI-derived instances of designated data types.
column8: Classification labels are homed at ID.AM-07 (Ex3). The relationship to PR.AA-05 is a prerequisite (precedes) relationship.

column2: Inventories of data and corresponding metadata for designated data types are maintained
column6: Verify that every model artifact publishes a version-controlled, machine-readable AI BOM listing datasets, weights, licenses, and data-origin statements.
column7: Listing datasets and data-origin statements in the AI BOM is one way to maintain data inventories with provenance metadata for the data behind each model.
column8: Matches ID.AM-07 Ex4 (track provenance). Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 CM-12 to ID.AM-07.

column2: Inventories of data and corresponding metadata for designated data types are maintained
column6: Verify that dataset lineage records each dataset and its components, including all transformations, augmentations, and merges.
column7: Recording the lineage of each training dataset and its components, including transformations, augmentations and merges, is one way to maintain detailed provenance metadata for training data.
column8: Matches ID.AM-07 Ex4 (track provenance). 'example of': source-level provenance and processing history are already required by v1.01-C1.1.2 (integral to); component-level lineage is a more detailed practice. No direct SP 800-53 precedent in NIST's CSF 2.0 informative references.

column2: Inventories of data and corresponding metadata for designated data types are maintained
column6: Verify that all labeling activities are recorded in logs.
column7: Recording labeling history is one way to maintain provenance metadata for training data, showing how each training label was produced or changed.
column8: Matches ID.AM-07 Ex4 (provenance). ML training labels are not the data-classification labels of Ex3.

column2: Inventories of data and corresponding metadata for designated data types are maintained
column6: Verify that every ingested document is tagged at write time with source, writer identity, and timestamp.
column7: Tagging every ingested document at write time with source, writer identity and timestamp is one way to maintain provenance and ownership metadata for knowledge-base data that feeds retrieval or memory.
column8: Matches ID.AM-07 Ex4 (provenance, data owner). 'example of': write-time tagging is one mechanism; provenance could also be kept in a separate ingestion record. No direct SP 800-53 precedent in NIST's CSF 2.0 informative references.

column2: Systems, hardware, software, services, and data are managed throughout their life cycles
column6: Verify that training data includes only features, attributes, and fields required for the model's stated purpose.
column7: Restricting training data to the features and fields required for the model's stated purpose is one way to manage AI data across its life cycle with cybersecurity in mind, limiting sensitive data exposed to extraction or leakage.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SI-12 (incl. SI-12(1) limit PII elements) to ID.AM-08. Data minimization is one life-cycle practice among several.

column2: Systems, hardware, software, services, and data are managed throughout their life cycles
column6: Verify that expired vectors are excluded from retrieval results.
column7: Excluding expired vectors from retrieval results is the AI-specific part of enforcing data retention for vector memory; without it ID.AM-08 is not met for RAG indices.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SI-12 to ID.AM-08. The requirement states the result, not a mechanism, hence integral to.

column2: Systems, hardware, software, services, and data are managed throughout their life cycles
column6: Verify that memory can be reset.
column7: A memory reset capability is one way to dispose of AI memory content at revocation or tenant offboarding, managing that data through its life cycle.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SI-12 to ID.AM-08.

column2: The cybersecurity risk to the organization, assets, and individuals is understood by the organization
Vulnerabilities in assets are identified, validated, and recorded
column6: Verify that models used in security-relevant decisions are evaluated for bias patterns.
column7: Evaluating models used in security-relevant decisions for bias patterns is one way to identify exploitable weaknesses, such as systematic blind spots attackers can use for evasion, in AI systems.
column8: Mixed purpose; only the security purpose (bias as an evasion weakness in security decisions) is mapped. Fairness aspects are outside CSF scope (see NIST AI RMF).

column2: Vulnerabilities in assets are identified, validated, and recorded
column6: Verify that prompt content classification is evaluated for unsupported languages.
column7: Evaluating prompt classification against unsupported, mixed and transliterated languages is one way to identify and validate a bypass weakness in the AI system's input screening controls.
column8: Mapped for the security purpose (language-based bypass of input controls); content-safety aspects are outside CSF scope.

column2: Vulnerabilities in assets are identified, validated, and recorded
column6: Verify that models undergo automated input validation testing, safety evaluation testing, and output sanitization testing before deployment.
column7: Testing models' input validation and output sanitization before deployment is one way to identify vulnerabilities in organization-developed AI systems.
column8: Matches ID.RA-01 Ex3 (test organization-developed software). Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SA-11(2) to ID.RA-01.

column2: Vulnerabilities in assets are identified, validated, and recorded
column6: Verify that models are evaluated against known adversarial attack techniques relevant to their modality.
column7: Evaluating models against known adversarial attack techniques for their modality is the AI-specific part of identifying vulnerabilities in assets; without it ID.RA-01 is not met for the model's attack surface.
column8: Matches ID.RA-01 Ex3 (test organization-developed software). Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 CA-8 and RA-5 to ID.RA-01.

column2: Vulnerabilities in assets are identified, validated, and recorded
column6: Verify that adversarial evaluation results are reported alongside results for the same tasks, scored the same way, with no attack applied.
column7: Reporting adversarial evaluation results next to no-attack results for the same tasks and scoring is one way to validate and record AI model vulnerabilities, separating attack-induced failures from ordinary errors.
column8: Supports the 'validated and recorded' part of ID.RA-01.

column2: Vulnerabilities in assets are identified, validated, and recorded
column6: Verify that membership-inference attack simulations demonstrate that attack accuracy does not exceed random guessing on evaluated data.
column7: Simulating membership-inference attacks to show attack accuracy does not exceed random guessing is one way to identify and validate a confidentiality vulnerability of the AI model.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 CA-8 (penetration testing) to ID.RA-01.

column2: Cyber threat intelligence is received from information sharing forums and sources
Internal and external threats to the organization are identified and recorded
Potential impacts and likelihoods of threats exploiting vulnerabilities are identified and recorded
Threats, vulnerabilities, likelihoods, and impacts are used to understand inherent risk and inform risk response prioritization
Risk responses are chosen, prioritized, planned, tracked, and communicated
Changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded, and tracked
column6: Verify that models subjected to post-training quantization are re-evaluated against the same safety and alignment test suite on the compressed artifact before deployment.
column7: Re-running the same test suite on a quantized model before deployment is one way to assess the risk impact of an AI model change, since quantization can weaken safeguards or hide backdoors.
column8: Prescribes a specific method (same suite on the compressed artifact); safety and alignment aspects are outside CSF scope. Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 CM-4 to ID.RA-07.

column2: Changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded, and tracked
column6: Verify that provider model, version, or routing changes trigger security re-evaluation before continued use.
column7: Assessing provider model, version or routing changes for security impact before continued use is the AI-specific part of assessing changes for risk impact; without it ID.RA-07 is not met for these changes.
column8: The requirement names no specific evaluation method. Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 CM-4 to ID.RA-07.

column2: Changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded, and tracked
column6: Verify that production deployments implement rollout mechanisms with automated rollback triggers.
column7: Rolling out model deployments in a controlled way with automated rollback triggers is one way to manage changes to production AI systems and to provide for rolling them back (ID.RA-07 Ex2).
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 CM-3 (configuration change control) to PR.PS-01 and ID.RA-07.

column2: Changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded, and tracked
column6: Verify that MCP clients maintain a snapshot of tool definitions and that any change to a tool definition triggers re-approval before the modified tool can be invoked.
column7: Re-approval of a changed MCP tool definition before use is one way to review and approve changes to third-party tools before they affect the AI system.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 CM-3 and CM-4 to ID.RA-07.

column2: Changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded, and tracked
column6: Verify that a version-controlled alignment test suite is run on every model update or release.
column7: Running a version-controlled alignment test suite, including jailbreak cases, on every model update or release is one way to assess model changes for security impact before they take effect.
column8: Mapped for the security purpose (jailbreak and policy-bypass regressions). Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 CM-4 (impact analyses) to ID.RA-07.

column2: Changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded, and tracked
column6: Verify that all model changes generate immutable audit records.
column7: Generating audit records for every model change is the AI-specific part of recording and tracking changes; without it ID.RA-07 is not met for model artifacts. Immutability additionally protects the change history against tampering.
column8: The requirement targets the change history of models. Precedent: SP 800-53 CM-3 -> ID.RA-07.

column2: Processes for receiving, analyzing, and responding to vulnerability disclosures are established
The authenticity and integrity of hardware and software are assessed prior to acquisition and use
column6: Verify that all model artifacts (weights, configurations, tokenizers, base models, fine-tunes, adapters, and safety/policy models) are cryptographically signed by authorized entities.
column7: Signing model artifacts by authorized entities is a prerequisite for assessing their authenticity and integrity before use; it is not itself the assessment.
column8: The assessment itself is covered by v1.01-C3.1.3. Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SI-7 to ID.RA-09.

column2: The authenticity and integrity of hardware and software are assessed prior to acquisition and use
column6: Verify that model cryptographic signatures are verified at deployment admission and on load.
column7: Verifying model signatures at deployment admission and on load is the AI-specific part of assessing software integrity and authenticity before use; without it ID.RA-09 is not met for deployed models.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SI-7 and SR-11 to ID.RA-09.

column2: The authenticity and integrity of hardware and software are assessed prior to acquisition and use
column6: Verify that models used in RLHF fine-tuning are versioned and integrity-verified before use in a training run.
column7: Verifying the integrity of reward and reference models before a training run is the AI-specific part of assessing software integrity before use; without it ID.RA-09 is not met for RLHF pipelines.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SI-7 and SA-10 to ID.RA-09.

column2: The authenticity and integrity of hardware and software are assessed prior to acquisition and use
column6: Verify that in multi-stage fine-tuning pipelines, each stage's output is integrity-verified before it is consumed by the next stage.
column7: Verifying each fine-tuning stage's output before the next stage consumes it is the AI-specific part of assessing software integrity before use; without it ID.RA-09 is not met for multi-stage pipelines.
column8: The requirement demands the assessment itself, without prescribing a technique. Precedent: SI-7, SA-10 -> ID.RA-09.

column2: The authenticity and integrity of hardware and software are assessed prior to acquisition and use
column6: Verify that workload attestation is performed before model loading to provide proof that the execution environment has not been tampered with.
column7: Attesting the execution environment before model loading is one way to assess the integrity of the hardware and software platform before an AI model is deployed on it.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SI-7 to ID.RA-09. Workload attestation is one specific technique, hence example of.

column2: The authenticity and integrity of hardware and software are assessed prior to acquisition and use
column6: Verify that AI accelerator (GPU) firmware is version-pinned, signed, and attested at boot.
column7: Verifying signed AI accelerator firmware through attestation at boot is one way to assess firmware integrity and authenticity before the accelerator is used.
column8: Integrity verification before use is the core of the requirement, version pinning is secondary. 'example of': boot-time attestation is one technique, consistent with v1.01-C4.1.3 and v1.01-C4.2.3. Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SI-7 to ID.RA-09.

column2: The authenticity and integrity of hardware and software are assessed prior to acquisition and use
column6: Verify that AI accelerator (GPU) integrity is validated using hardware-based attestation mechanisms before each workload executes.
column7: Validating AI accelerator integrity with hardware-based attestation before each workload is one way to assess hardware integrity before use.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SI-7 to ID.RA-09. Per-workload hardware attestation is a specific technique beyond boot-time checks, hence example of.

column2: The authenticity and integrity of hardware and software are assessed prior to acquisition and use
column6: Verify that models deployed to edge or mobile devices are cryptographically signed during packaging, and that the on-device runtime validates these signatures or checksums before loading or inference.
column7: Validating signatures or checksums of models before loading on edge or mobile devices is the AI-specific part of assessing software integrity before use; without it ID.RA-09 is not met for on-device models.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SI-7 to ID.RA-09. Signing at packaging is the prerequisite contained in the same requirement.

column2: The authenticity and integrity of hardware and software are assessed prior to acquisition and use
column6: Verify that models are scanned for malicious code before import.
column7: Scanning models for malicious code before import is one way to assess the cybersecurity of acquired AI software before use, since serialized models can carry executable payloads.
column8: The scan is an assessment before use. Matches ID.RA-09 Ex1. 'example of': restricting model loading to serialization formats that cannot execute code (v1.01-C4.1.2) is an alternative. Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SR-11 to ID.RA-09.

column2: The authenticity and integrity of hardware and software are assessed prior to acquisition and use
column6: Verify that every third-party model artifact can be integrity-verified.
column7: Ensuring every third-party model artifact can be integrity-verified is the AI-specific part of assessing acquired software integrity before use; without it ID.RA-09 is not met for third-party models.
column8: The requirement leaves the verification mechanism open, hence integral to. Precedent: SR-11, SI-7 -> ID.RA-09.

column2: The authenticity and integrity of hardware and software are assessed prior to acquisition and use
column6: Verify that models pass a behavioral acceptance test suite before being promoted to any non-development environment.
column7: A behavioral acceptance test suite run before promotion is one way to assess acquired models for hidden or malicious behavior before use, complementing integrity and code scanning.
column8: The section targets third-party models before use. Safety and alignment tests are outside CSF scope. Precedent: SA-11 -> ID.RA-09.

column2: The authenticity and integrity of hardware and software are assessed prior to acquisition and use
column6: Verify that AI BOMs are cryptographically signed before deployment.
column7: Signing AI BOMs is a prerequisite for assessing the authenticity and integrity of model components before use; it is not itself the assessment.
column8: Same pattern as model-artifact signing (v1.01-C3.1.2). Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SI-7 to ID.RA-09.

column2: The authenticity and integrity of hardware and software are assessed prior to acquisition and use
column6: Verify that MCP components are obtained only from trusted sources and cryptographically verified.
column7: Obtaining MCP components only from trusted sources and cryptographically verifying them is the AI-specific part of assessing software authenticity and integrity before use; without it ID.RA-09 is not met for MCP servers and tools.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SR-11 and SI-7 to ID.RA-09.

column2: Critical suppliers are assessed prior to acquisition
Improvements to organizational cybersecurity risk management processes, procedures and activities are identified across all CSF Functions
Improvements are identified from evaluations
Improvements are identified from security tests and exercises, including those done in coordination with suppliers and relevant third parties
Improvements are identified from execution of operational processes, procedures, and activities
Incident response plans and other cybersecurity plans that affect operations are established, communicated, maintained, and improved
Safeguards to manage the organization's cybersecurity risks are used
Access to physical and logical assets is limited to authorized users, services, and hardware and  managed commensurate with the assessed risk of unauthorized access
Identities and credentials for authorized users, services, and hardware are managed by the organization
column6: Verify that cryptographic key material or credentials used to issue approvals are isolated from the agent runtime, and that the runtime can neither read them nor use them to issue approvals.
column7: Keeping approval-signing key material and credentials outside the agent runtime is one key-management practice that protects the credentials of the approval service from misuse by the agent (Ex2).
column8: Precedent: IA-5 (authenticator management) -> PR.AA-01.

column2: Identities and credentials for authorized users, services, and hardware are managed by the organization
column6: Verify that each agent instance has a unique cryptographic identity and authenticates as a first-class principal to downstream systems.
column7: Giving each agent instance a unique cryptographic identity is the agent-specific part of managing identities and credentials for services; without it, agents share or borrow credentials and PR.AA-01 is not met for agents.
column8: Precedent: IA-4, IA-9 -> PR.AA-01. Unique identity is the requirement's main object.

column2: Identities and credentials for authorized users, services, and hardware are managed by the organization
column6: Verify that agent identity credentials rotate on a defined schedule.
column7: Rotating agent identity credentials on a defined schedule is one credential-management practice (Ex2) that limits how long stolen agent credentials remain usable.
column8: Precedent: IA-5 (authenticator management) -> PR.AA-01.

column2: Identities and credentials for authorized users, services, and hardware are managed by the organization
column6: Verify that secrets and credentials required by an agent at runtime are not exposed within the model's observable context, including the context window, system prompts, or tool call parameters.
column7: Supplying agent credentials outside the model's observable context is one credential-handling practice that protects agent credentials from disclosure through the model.
column8: Precedent: IA-5 (authenticator management) -> PR.AA-01.

column2: Identities and credentials for authorized users, services, and hardware are managed by the organization
column6: Verify that MCP servers acting as OAuth 2.1 resource servers do not store or persist access tokens or user credentials.
column7: Not storing or persisting access tokens and user credentials in MCP resource servers is one way to manage credentials so they cannot be harvested from the tool layer of an AI system.
column8: 'example of': credential non-persistence is one design choice; protected storage is an alternative. Precedent: IA-5 -> PR.AA-01.

column2: Identities and credentials for authorized users, services, and hardware are managed by the organization
column6: Verify that MCP clients bind persisted OAuth client credentials to the issuing authorization server and do not present them to a different authorization server.
column7: Binding persisted OAuth client credentials of MCP clients to their issuing authorization server is one credential-management practice that keeps these credentials from being disclosed to a different authorization server.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 IA-5 (authenticator management) to PR.AA-01. 'example of': a specific protection against authorization-server mix-up; other credential-handling designs can also meet PR.AA-01.

column2: Identities are proofed and bound to credentials based on the context of interactions
Users, services, and hardware are authenticated
column6: Verify that accelerator interconnects are restricted to approved topologies and authenticated endpoints.
column7: Authenticating endpoints on accelerator interconnects is one way to authenticate AI hardware before it exchanges data with other accelerators.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 IA-3 to PR.AA-03.

column2: Users, services, and hardware are authenticated
column6: Verify that edge AI devices authenticate to central infrastructure using strong authentication mechanisms.
column7: Strong authentication of edge AI devices to central infrastructure is the AI-specific instance of authenticating hardware; without it PR.AA-03 is not met for edge AI deployments.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 IA-3 to PR.AA-03. The mechanism is left open, hence integral to.

column2: Users, services, and hardware are authenticated
column6: Verify that high-risk AI operations (model deployment, weight export, training data access, production configuration changes) require step-up authentication.
column7: Requiring step-up authentication before high-risk AI operations such as model deployment or weight export is one way to authenticate users commensurate with risk.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 IA-11 (re-authentication) to PR.AA-03 (Ex3: reauthenticate based on risk).

column2: Users, services, and hardware are authenticated
column6: Verify that AI agents in federated or multi-system deployments authenticate using short-lived, minimal-scoped, cryptographically signed tokens.
column7: Token-based authentication of AI agents in federated or multi-system deployments is one way to authenticate services.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 IA-9 to PR.AA-03.

column2: Users, services, and hardware are authenticated
column6: Verify that each agent instance has a unique cryptographic identity and authenticates as a first-class principal to downstream systems.
column7: Requiring each agent to authenticate as a first-class principal to downstream systems is the agent-specific instance of authenticating services; without it, downstream systems cannot authenticate the agents acting on them.
column8: Precedent: IA-9 (service identification and authentication) -> PR.AA-03.

column2: Users, services, and hardware are authenticated
column6: Verify that MCP servers validate access tokens for each request and do not rely on transport security alone.
column7: Validating the access token on every request, rather than trusting the transport, is how MCP servers authenticate their callers; without it callers of MCP tools are not authenticated.
column8: The requirement is about authenticating every request, while v1.01-C10.2.2 covers how tokens are validated.

column2: Users, services, and hardware are authenticated
column6: Verify that MCP servers do not use form-mode elicitation to request secrets or payment credentials, and that in URL-mode elicitation the user completing the flow is the same user who initiated it.
column7: Confirming that the user completing a URL-mode elicitation is the user who initiated it is one authentication check that prevents binding one user's credentials to another user's session.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 IA-2 to PR.AA-03.

column2: Users, services, and hardware are authenticated
column6: Verify that MCP servers exclude end-user credentials and personal data from URL-mode elicitation URLs, and do not issue URLs that are pre-authenticated to a protected resource.
column7: Not issuing URLs that are pre-authenticated to a protected resource ensures the user completing the flow must still authenticate, one way to keep elicitation links from acting as bearer credentials.
column8: Precedent: IA-2 -> PR.AA-03.

column2: Identity assertions are protected, conveyed, and verified
column6: Verify that AI agents in federated or multi-system deployments authenticate using short-lived, minimal-scoped, cryptographically signed tokens.
column7: Using short-lived, minimally scoped, cryptographically signed tokens is one way to protect and verify identity assertions exchanged by AI agents across federated systems.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 IA-13 to PR.AA-04 (Ex2, Ex3). The requirement specifies assertion properties.

column2: Identity assertions are protected, conveyed, and verified
column6: Verify that approvals are cryptographically bound to action parameters, requester identity, execution context, and a unique single-use nonce, and are rejected if any bound value changes or the nonce is reused.
column7: Cryptographically binding approvals to action parameters, requester identity, execution context and a single-use nonce is one way to protect and verify approval assertions against replay, theft and parameter swap.
column8: Precedent: IA-13 (assertions and access tokens) -> PR.AA-04, PR.AA-05. The requirement protects and verifies the approval artifact.

column2: Identity assertions are protected, conveyed, and verified
column6: Verify that when an agent acts on a user's behalf, the runtime propagates an integrity-protected, scope-limited token that carries the user's authorization context and is enforced at every downstream call.
column7: Propagating an integrity-protected token with the user's authorization context to every downstream call is how agents acting for a user protect, convey and verify the delegated assertion; without it PR.AA-04 is not met for delegated calls.
column8: Precedent: IA-13 -> PR.AA-04, PR.AA-05. The requirement centers on the delegated token.

column2: Identity assertions are protected, conveyed, and verified
column6: Verify that MCP servers validate access tokens for each request and do not rely on transport security alone.
column7: Per-request token validation is the verification of the access token conveyed to the MCP server; an unverified token leaves PR.AA-04 unmet for MCP calls.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 IA-13 (identity providers and authorization servers) to PR.AA-04.

column2: Identity assertions are protected, conveyed, and verified
column6: Verify that MCP servers validate the presented access token's issuer, audience, expiration, and scope claims in accordance with OAuth 2.1.
column7: Validating issuer, audience, expiration and scope claims of tokens presented to MCP servers per OAuth 2.1 is the standards-based verification of assertions that PR.AA-04 Ex3 describes.
column8: Precedent: IA-13 -> PR.AA-04.

column2: Identity assertions are protected, conveyed, and verified
column6: Verify that MCP servers only accept tokens explicitly issued for them, and do not pass tokens issued for other services through to downstream APIs.
column7: Accepting only tokens issued for the MCP server and not passing them through to downstream APIs is part of verifying and protecting assertions; accepting foreign-audience tokens means assertions are not verified.
column8: Precedent: IA-13 -> PR.AA-04.

column2: Identity assertions are protected, conveyed, and verified
column6: Verify that access tokens between the MCP client and server are sender-constrained using mTLS or DPoP.
column7: Sender-constraining MCP access tokens with mTLS or DPoP is one way to protect conveyed assertions against theft and replay by parties other than the legitimate MCP client.
column8: 'example of': mTLS/DPoP are specific mechanisms. Precedent: IA-13 -> PR.AA-04.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that labeling platforms enforce access controls that restrict who can create, modify, or approve annotations.
column7: Enforcing access control on who can create, modify or approve annotations is the AI-specific part of enforcing authorizations with separation of duties for labeling platforms; without it PR.AA-05 is not met there.
column8: Separating create/modify from approve rights reflects separation of duties. Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 AC-3 and AC-5 to PR.AA-05.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that every AI resource (datasets, endpoints, vector collections, embedding indices, compute instances) enforces access controls with explicit allow-lists and default-deny policies.
column7: Enforcing allow-list, default-deny access control on every AI resource (datasets, endpoints, vector collections, compute) is the AI-specific part of enforcing least-privilege authorizations; without it PR.AA-05 is not met for the AI system.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 AC-3 and AC-6 to PR.AA-05.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that retrieval pipelines (e.g., RAG queries, embedding lookups) enforce the end-user's authorization context at each retrieval and assembly stage, rather than relying solely on the service account's permissions.
column7: Enforcing the end user's authorization at every retrieval and assembly stage is the AI-specific part of enforcing access permissions; without it a RAG pipeline returns data to unentitled callers via its service account.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 AC-3 to PR.AA-05 (Ex2: requester attributes in authorization decisions).

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that sensitive data is retrieved via retrieval pipelines (e.g., RAG queries, embedding lookups) to prevent permanent storage in models.
column7: Keeping sensitive data in retrieval stores is a prerequisite for enforcing per-caller access permissions on it; it is not itself the enforcement.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 AC-3 to PR.AA-05. The enforcement itself is covered by v1.01-C5.2.2.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that post-inference filtering mechanisms prevent responses from including data that the requester is not authorized to receive.
column7: Filtering model responses after inference against the requester's entitlements is one way to enforce access permissions on data an AI system could otherwise disclose to unauthorized users.
column8: Authorization-aware output filtering is homed at PR.AA-05, not PR.DS-02. Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 AC-3 to PR.AA-05.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that the policy decision point for agent authorization is isolated from the agent's execution environment.
column7: Isolating the agent authorization policy decision point from the agent's execution environment is one design pattern that keeps authorization enforcement intact when the agent itself is compromised.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 AC-3 to PR.AA-05. Architectural pattern, hence example of.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that privileged access to model weights, training pipelines, and production AI configuration is granted just in time, with a defined maximum session duration and automatic expiry. Zero Standing Privilege (ZSP) to these resources is encouraged.
column7: Granting privileged access to model weights, training pipelines and production AI configuration just in time with automatic expiry is one way to restrict privileges to the minimum necessary.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 AC-6 to PR.AA-05 (Ex3). JIT access is one least-privilege technique.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that data classification labels propagate to downstream resources (embeddings, prompt caches, model outputs).
column7: Labels on derived AI resources are a prerequisite for enforcing label-based access permissions on embeddings, caches and outputs; propagating them is not itself the enforcement.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 AC-16 (security and privacy attributes) to PR.AA-05.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that retrieval operations enforce scope constraints.
column7: Enforcing scope constraints on every retrieval from vector collections and memory is the AI-specific part of enforcing access permissions; without it PR.AA-05 is not met for RAG indices.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 AC-3 to PR.AA-05.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that the agent runtime blocks execution of privileged or irreversible actions until explicit human approval is received and verified.
column7: Blocking privileged or irreversible agent actions until a verified human approval is received is one way to enforce authorization for the high-impact actions an AI agent attempts.
column8: Precedent: AC-3/AC-6 -> PR.AA-05. Human approval is one enforcement pattern; denying or narrowly scoping such actions could also achieve the outcome.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that approval requests display canonicalized and complete action parameters, such as diffs, commands, recipients, amounts, resources, and scopes, without truncation or unsafe transformation.
column7: Showing approvers canonicalized, complete action parameters ensures the human authorization decision refers to the action actually executed; it is one safeguard for authorizations granted through agent approval gates.
column8: Defeats approval substitution (bait-and-switch). Mapped to PR.AA-05 because the approval is the authorization step for the action.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that each high-impact action has a trusted reversibility classification, such as read-only, reversible, externally reversible, or irreversible.
column7: Assigning each high-impact agent action a trusted reversibility classification is a prerequisite for authorization rules that depend on action impact; the classification itself does not enforce any access decision.
column8: Precedent: AC-16 (security attributes) -> PR.AA-05. Declaring the classification precedes enforcing it (enforcement: v1.01-C9.2.4).

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that the agent runtime enforces reversibility classifications by blocking, requiring approval, or restricting actions based on their impact and ability to be reversed.
column7: Enforcing reversibility classifications at runtime by blocking, requiring approval or restricting actions is one way to apply authorization decisions that take attributes of the requested action into account (Ex2).
column8: Precedent: AC-3 and AC-16 -> PR.AA-05. Reversibility-based gating is one risk-tiered enforcement approach.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that any self-modification capability (e.g., prompt rewriting, tool-list changes, parameter updates) is restricted by boundaries that are enforced by the runtime and cannot be changed or bypassed by the agent.
column7: Preventing an agent from extending its own tool list or parameters is one way to stop self-granted privilege escalation, keeping agent entitlements at the authorized minimum (Ex3).
column8: Precedent: AC-6 (least privilege) -> PR.AA-05.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that agentic systems include an AI-augmented review of planned high-risk actions before execution that adds to, and does not replace, the deterministic policy gate.
column7: An AI-augmented review of planned high-risk actions, layered on the deterministic policy gate, is one additional mechanism for deciding whether an agent action may proceed.
column8: The review sits in the pre-execution approval path and adds to, not replaces, policy enforcement.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that approvals are cryptographically bound to action parameters, requester identity, execution context, and a unique single-use nonce, and are rejected if any bound value changes or the nonce is reused.
column7: Rejecting approvals whose bound values changed or whose nonce is reused ensures an agent executes only the exact action that was authorized, one way to enforce approval-based authorizations.
column8: Precedent: IA-13 -> PR.AA-05.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that cryptographic key material or credentials used to issue approvals are isolated from the agent runtime, and that the runtime can neither read them nor use them to issue approvals.
column7: Isolating approval-issuing keys and credentials from the agent runtime prevents the actor from approving its own actions; without it, separation of duties between agent and approver is not achieved for cryptographic approval gates.
column8: Precedent: AC-5 (separation of duties) -> PR.AA-05. The protected outcome is separation of duties.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that approval gates for multi-step or multi-agent action chains enforce the highest-impact reversibility classification present anywhere in the chain, where the chain is established by a component outside the control of the agent being gated.
column7: Enforcing the highest-impact classification present anywhere in a multi-step or multi-agent chain, with the chain defined outside the gated agent, is one way to prevent risk laundering through delegated sub-actions.
column8: Precedent: AC-3/AC-6 -> PR.AA-05. Approval gates are treated as authorization controls.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that agent execution which would exceed the approved action chain is blocked until a new approval is obtained, and that the new approval enforces the highest-impact reversibility classification present across the cumulative chain.
column7: Blocking agent execution that exceeds the approved action chain until a new approval is obtained is one way to keep an agent within its granted authorization, so stale approvals cannot become blanket authority.
column8: Precedent: AC-3 -> PR.AA-05. Approval gates are treated as authorization controls.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that each tool/plugin executes in a least-privilege sandbox or is otherwise isolated from model operations.
column7: Running each tool in a least-privilege sandbox is one way to restrict the access and privileges of AI tools to the minimum necessary (Ex3).
column8: Precedent: AC-6 (least privilege) -> PR.AA-05.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that tool manifests declare required privileges, resource limits, and output validation requirements.
column7: Declaring required privileges, resource limits and output validation in tool manifests is a prerequisite for enforcing least privilege on AI tools; the declaration does not itself enforce any access decision.
column8: Declaration precedes enforcement (v1.01-C9.3.4). Precedent for the enforced outcome: AC-6 -> PR.AA-05.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that the runtime enforces the privileges, resource limits, and output-validation requirements declared in tool manifests.
column7: Enforcing manifest-declared privileges at runtime is one way to restrict each AI tool's access to the minimum necessary, turning declared least privilege into enforced authorization.
column8: Privilege enforcement is the leading purpose. The output-validation part overlaps v1.01-C9.3.2 (PR.DS-10).

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that agent actions are authorized against fine-grained policies enforced by the runtime that restrict which tools an agent may invoke, and which parameter values it may supply.
column7: Runtime-enforced fine-grained policies on which tools an agent may invoke and with which parameter values are the agent-specific enforcement of defined authorizations and least privilege; without them PR.AA-05 is not met for agent actions.
column8: Precedent: AC-3, AC-6 -> PR.AA-05.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that when an agent acts on a user's behalf, the runtime propagates an integrity-protected, scope-limited token that carries the user's authorization context and is enforced at every downstream call.
column7: Scope-limiting the delegated token and enforcing it at every downstream call is one way to keep agent actions within the user's own entitlements (least privilege).
column8: Precedent: IA-13 -> PR.AA-05.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that all access control decisions are enforced by application logic or a policy engine, never by the AI model itself.
column7: Keeping all access control decisions in application logic or a policy engine, never in the model, makes authorization enforcement deterministic; if the model decides access, authorizations are not reliably enforced and PR.AA-05 is not met.
column8: Precedent: AC-3 (access enforcement) -> PR.AA-05.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that inter-agent task delegation is restricted by an explicit authorization policy.
column7: Restricting inter-agent task delegation by an explicit authorization policy is the multi-agent instance of defining and enforcing authorizations; without it, agents can hand tasks to peers outside policy and PR.AA-05 is not met.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 AC-3 and AC-6 to PR.AA-05.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that long-running agent sessions re-evaluate current backend authorization policy on every privileged action.
column7: Re-evaluating current backend authorization policy on every privileged action in long-running agent sessions is one continuous-enforcement technique that applies revoked or changed privileges promptly (Ex1).
column8: Precedent: AC-3 -> PR.AA-05. Short-lived grants or revocation propagation are alternative techniques.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that authority derived through delegation never exceeds the delegating agent's current authority.
column7: Ensuring delegated authority never exceeds the delegating agent's current authority is the delegation-specific form of least privilege; without it, delegation chains escalate privileges and PR.AA-05 is not met.
column8: Precedent: AC-6 (least privilege) -> PR.AA-05.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that when a human-approval gate is not satisfied within the defined approval time, the system blocks the pending action.
column7: Blocking a pending action when its human approval is not given in time makes the approval gate fail closed, one way to ensure high-impact agent actions run only with an affirmative authorization.
column8: Approval gates are treated as authorization controls (AC-3 -> PR.AA-05). A fail-closed timeout is one design choice.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that locally launched MCP servers run in a least-privilege sandbox with restricted file system, network, and system access.
column7: Running local MCP server processes with least privilege is one way to restrict the access and privileges of AI tool servers to the minimum necessary (Ex3).
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 AC-6 (least privilege) to PR.AA-05.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that MCP tools/list returns only tools permitted by the requester's authorized scopes, and that list responses vary only by authorization context, never by connection.
column7: Filtering MCP tools/list results by the requester's authorized scopes, never by connection, is one way to apply least privilege to tool discovery in an AI system.
column8: 'example of': authorization is still enforced at invocation (v1.01-C10.2.5); list filtering adds minimal exposure. Precedent: AC-3 -> PR.AA-05.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that MCP servers enforce access control on every tool invocation, validating that the user's access token authorizes both the requested tool and the specific argument values supplied.
column7: Enforcing access control on every MCP tool invocation, including the specific argument values, is the enforcement of authorizations for AI tool use; without it PR.AA-05 is not met for MCP tools.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 AC-3 to PR.AA-05; argument-level checks reflect Ex2 (attributes of the requested resource).

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that MCP proxy servers using a shared upstream OAuth client identity do not allow a requesting MCP client to inherit authorization established for a different MCP client.
column7: Preventing an MCP client from inheriting authorization granted to another client behind a shared upstream OAuth identity is the enforcement of per-client authorizations; without it MCP proxies act as confused deputies.
column8: Precedent: AC-3 -> PR.AA-05.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that MCP clients bind each approved MCP server's granted consent and authorization to the connection endpoint approved for that server, and require user re-approval before any further interaction once that endpoint changes.
column7: Binding consent and authorization to the approved MCP server endpoint, with re-approval on change, keeps granted authorizations scoped to the resource they were granted for; otherwise an unapproved endpoint inherits them.
column8: Precedent: AC-3 -> PR.AA-05; reflects Ex2 (attributes of the requested resource).

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that MCP clients require explicit user consent and display the full URL before opening any URL-mode elicitation target, and do not pre-fetch the URL or its metadata.
column7: Requiring explicit user consent with the full URL displayed before an MCP client opens a server-requested elicitation target is one human approval gate for actions initiated by an MCP server.
column8: The core control is user approval. Precedent: AC-3 -> PR.AA-05.

column2: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
column6: Verify that autonomous action triggers include proactive behavior-pattern analysis, security evaluation, and threat-landscape assessment.
column7: Requiring a security evaluation before an autonomous action is triggered is one way to make authorization decisions for agent actions risk-aware, taking attributes of the requesting agent and requested action into account.
column8: Matches PR.AA-05 Ex2 (attribute-aware authorization decisions). Precedent: SP 800-53 AC-24 -> PR.AA-05.

column2: Physical access to assets is managed, monitored, and enforced commensurate with risk
The organization's personnel are provided with cybersecurity awareness and training so that they can perform their cybersecurity-related tasks
Personnel are provided with awareness and training so that they possess the knowledge and skills to perform general tasks with cybersecurity risks in mind
Individuals in specialized roles are provided with awareness and training so that they possess the knowledge and skills to perform relevant tasks with cybersecurity risks in mind
Data are managed consistent with the organization's risk strategy to protect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information
The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected
column6: Verify that data integrity is provided when training data is stored and transferred.
column7: Providing integrity for stored training data is the AI-specific part of protecting data at rest; tampering with stored datasets poisons the model, so PR.DS-01 is not met for the AI system without it.
column8: Stored datasets are the dominant poisoning surface. Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SC-28 and SI-7 to PR.DS-01.

column2: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected
column6: Verify that cryptographic integrity is applied to labeling artifacts.
column7: Applying cryptographic integrity protection (hashes or signatures) to labeling artifacts is one way to protect the integrity of stored AI training data.
column8: Matches PR.DS-01 Ex1; cryptography is one mechanism, integrity could also be protected otherwise (e.g., immutable storage). Precedent: SC-28, SI-7 -> PR.DS-01.

column2: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected
column6: Verify that sensitive information in labels is redacted, anonymized, or encrypted before being used in any labeling artifact.
column7: Redacting, anonymizing or encrypting sensitive information before it enters labeling artifacts is one way to protect the confidentiality of stored AI training data handled by annotators.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SC-28 to PR.DS-01. The requirement lists alternative techniques, each one way to meet the outcome.

column2: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected
column6: Verify that all model artifacts (weights, configurations, tokenizers, base models, fine-tunes, adapters, and safety/policy models) are cryptographically signed by authorized entities.
column7: Cryptographically signing model artifacts (weights, configurations, tokenizers, adapters, safety models) is one way to protect the integrity of stored AI artifacts, as PR.DS-01 Ex1 names digital signatures.
column8: Signing directly provides tamper evidence for stored artifacts, whereas its role for ID.RA-09 is only preparatory. Precedent: SI-7 -> PR.DS-01.

column2: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected
column6: Verify that model weights and sensitive parameters stored locally are encrypted using hardware-backed key stores or secure enclaves.
column7: Encrypting locally stored model weights with hardware-backed key stores or secure enclaves is one way to protect the confidentiality of AI data at rest.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SC-28 to PR.DS-01 (Ex1).

column2: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected
column6: Verify that models packaged within mobile, IoT, or embedded applications are encrypted at rest, and decrypted only inside a trusted runtime or secure enclave, preventing direct extraction from the app package or filesystem.
column7: Encrypting models packaged in mobile, IoT or embedded applications is one way to protect model weights at rest against extraction from the app package or filesystem.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SC-28 to PR.DS-01. The stated aim is preventing extraction at rest.

column2: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected
column6: Verify that sensitive data is retrieved via retrieval pipelines (e.g., RAG queries, embedding lookups) to prevent permanent storage in models.
column7: Retrieving sensitive data at query time instead of training it into model weights is one way to keep it in protected stores rather than in a model artifact where its confidentiality cannot be controlled.
column8: The relationship to PR.AA-05 is a prerequisite (precedes) relationship. Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SC-28 to PR.DS-01. Architectural pattern, hence example of.

column2: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected
column6: Verify that AI BOMs are cryptographically signed before deployment.
column7: Cryptographically signing AI BOMs before deployment is one way to protect the integrity of stored supply-chain metadata for AI systems.
column8: Signing directly provides tamper evidence (PR.DS-01 Ex1), whereas for ID.RA-09 it is only preparatory. Precedent: SI-7 -> PR.DS-01.

column2: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected
column6: Verify that vector identifiers and namespaces enforce uniqueness per tenant and prevent cross-tenant collisions.
column7: Enforcing tenant-unique vector identifiers and namespaces is one way to protect the integrity and confidentiality of vectors stored for multiple tenants against overwrite, aliasing and cross-tenant exposure.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SC-4 to PR.DS-01. Stored vectors are data at rest, so PR.DS-01 rather than PR.DS-10.

column2: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected
column6: Verify that document metadata tags are immutable after the initial write.
column7: Making document metadata tags in vector stores immutable after the initial write is one way to protect the integrity of stored metadata such as tenant, classification, provenance and expiry.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SI-7 to PR.DS-01. Write-once metadata is one integrity technique; hashes or signatures are alternatives.

column2: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected
column6: Verify that sensitive fields are detected before embedding and are masked, tokenized, or dropped.
column7: Detecting sensitive fields and masking, tokenizing or dropping them before embedding is one way to protect the confidentiality of sensitive data that would otherwise persist in vector stores.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SC-28 to PR.DS-01. Masking and tokenization are specific techniques, hence example of.

column2: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected
column6: Verify that no component reachable from agent execution can write agent outputs or tool outputs to trusted agent memory without explicit source validation.
column7: Blocking unvalidated writes to persistent agent memory is one way to protect the integrity of AI data at rest against memory poisoning.
column8: The protected object is persistent trusted memory (data at rest). Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SI-7 to PR.DS-01.

column2: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected
column6: Verify that agent state persisted between invocations is integrity-protected.
column7: Integrity-protecting agent state persisted between invocations, such as goals, memory and partial results, is the agent-specific part of protecting data-at-rest integrity; without it, persisted state can be poisoned and PR.DS-01 is not met.
column8: Precedent: SC-28 and SI-7 -> PR.DS-01. The requirement names no specific technique.

column2: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected
column6: Verify that training on sensitive datasets employs differentially-private optimization.
column7: Using differentially private optimization when training on sensitive datasets is one way to protect the confidentiality of that data, which could otherwise be recovered from the stored model.
column8: No SP 800-53 precedent in NIST's CSF 2.0 informative references.

column2: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-in-transit are protected
column6: Verify that data integrity is provided when training data is stored and transferred.
column7: Providing integrity for training data while it is transferred is the AI-specific part of protecting data in transit; without it PR.DS-02 is not met for training-data flows.
column8: The requirement names no technique, so it is integral to both data-at-rest and data-in-transit outcomes. Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SC-8 to PR.DS-02.

column2: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-in-transit are protected
column6: Verify that output filters detect and block responses that disclose system prompt content or backend data.
column7: Detecting and blocking responses that disclose system prompt content or backend data is one way to prevent sensitive data from leaving the AI system in outbound communications.

column8: Poisoning detection is named first, consistent with v1.01-C1.3.1. Precedent: SI-4 -> DE.CM-09.

column2: Computing hardware and software, runtime environments, and their data are monitored to find potentially adverse events
column6: Verify that the system detects and alerts on known jailbreak patterns, prompt injection attempts, and adversarial inputs.
column7: Detecting jailbreak patterns, prompt-injection attempts and adversarial inputs is the AI-specific part of monitoring runtime environments and their data for adverse events; without it DE.CM-09 is not met for the model's primary attack vector.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 SI-4 to DE.CM-09; model inputs are the AI analogue of Ex1 common attack vectors.

column2: Computing hardware and software, runtime environments, and their data are monitored to find potentially adverse events
column6: Verify that LLM API traffic is monitored for covert-channel indicators and communication signatures to identify malware and command-and-control (C2) activity.
column7: Inspecting LLM API traffic for malware communication signatures is one way to monitor a common attack vector for malware that abuses AI services for command and control.
column8: Matches DE.CM-09 Ex1 (monitor common attack vectors to detect malware). Precedent: SP 800-53 SI-4 -> DE.CM-09.

column2: Computing hardware and software, runtime environments, and their data are monitored to find potentially adverse events
column6: Verify that data drift detection monitors input distribution changes that may impact model performance, using statistically validated methods matched to the input data type (e.g., KS test or PSI for tabular numeric features, embedding-distance metrics for text or image).
column7: Statistically monitoring input-distribution drift is one way to monitor the AI system's runtime data for potentially adverse events, such as adversarially shaped or poisoned input streams.
column8: Mapped only for the security purpose stated in the C12.3 section description (security-relevant behavioral shifts); drift monitoring for model performance alone is AI trustworthiness (NIST AI RMF). Precedent: SI-4 -> DE.CM-09.

Responses to detected cybersecurity incidents are managed
The incident response plan is executed in coordination with relevant third parties once an incident is declared
Incident reports are triaged and validated
Incidents are categorized and prioritized
Incidents are escalated or elevated as needed
The criteria for initiating incident recovery are applied
Investigations are conducted to ensure effective response and support forensics and recovery activities
Analysis is performed to establish what has taken place during an incident and the root cause of the incident
Actions performed during an investigation are recorded, and the records' integrity and provenance are preserved
column6: Verify that kill-switch activations and override commands are logged.
column7: Automatically logging kill-switch activations and overrides is one way to record response actions taken on an AI agent during an incident, showing who halted, resumed or overrode it and when.
column8: Matches RS.AN-06 Ex1 (responders record their actions); responders could record actions by other means. Precedent: SP 800-53 AU-7 and IR-4 -> RS.AN-06.

column2: Incident data and metadata are collected, and their integrity and provenance are preserved
column6: Verify that quarantined content is retained but excluded from all retrieval results.
column7: Retaining quarantined AI content instead of deleting it is one way to preserve incident data for analysis of memory or RAG poisoning.
column8: Precedent: NIST maps SP 800-53 IR-4 to RS.AN-07. Integrity and chain of custody are not demanded, hence example of.

Response activities are coordinated with internal and external stakeholders as required by laws, regulations, or policies
